paragraphs.title: The Poor Person’s Distress and Prayer

easy.explanation: The psalm begins, “Hear my prayer, O LORD.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask the LORD to hear?

easy.explanation: He asks the LORD to answer him quickly in the day of trouble.
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask the LORD to do when he calls?

easy.explanation: He says, “I am as a sparrow alone upon the house top.”
easy.q: What bird does the psalmist compare himself to when alone on the housetop?

answers: His heart is smitten and withered like grass
He is preparing for a feast
medium.explanation: His severe sorrow causes him to forget to eat.
medium.q: Why does the psalmist say that he forgets to eat his bread?

medium.explanation: The image describes a body weakened by grief and suffering.
medium.q: What does the phrase “my bones cleave to my skin” suggest?

medium.explanation: He says, “I have eaten ashes like bread.”
medium.q: What has the psalmist eaten like bread?

challenge.explanation: His body withers, and his days are like a declining shadow.
challenge.q: What common idea connects the descriptions of the psalmist’s body and his days?

answers: His suffering includes public reproach and hostility
His enemies have begun to pray
challenge.explanation: His enemies reproach him and are angry against him.
challenge.q: What does the mention of the psalmist’s enemies add to the description of his distress?

answers: Smoke, ashes, withering grass, and a fading shadow
challenge.explanation: These images emphasize sorrow, weakness, and passing life.
challenge.q: Which group of images is repeated in this passage?

paragraphs.title: The Eternal God and Mercy for Zion

easy.explanation: The psalmist says, “But thou, O LORD, shalt endure for ever.”
The verse says, “Thou shalt arise, and have mercy upon Zion.”
easy.q: Upon whom will the LORD have mercy?

easy.explanation: The LORD will appear in His glory when Zion is rebuilt.
easy.q: What will appear when the LORD builds up Zion?

answers: There is no longer any need for prayer
medium.explanation: The psalm says, “the set time, is come.”
medium.q: Why is the time right for the LORD to show favour to Zion?

answers: They take pleasure in them and favour them
medium.explanation: The servants take pleasure in Zion’s stones and favour its dust.
medium.q: What do the LORD’s servants feel about Zion’s stones and dust?

answers: To regard with kindness and approval
medium.explanation: The context shows affection and concern for Zion.
medium.q: In this passage, what does “to favour” mean?

answers: Human life passes away, but the LORD endures forever
Human life is eternal, but the LORD passes away
challenge.explanation: The LORD endures forever while human days are short and fading.
challenge.q: What is the main contrast between human life and the LORD in this section?

challenge.explanation: The verse directly connects Zion’s rebuilding with the LORD appearing in glory.
challenge.q: How is the rebuilding of Zion related to the LORD’s glory?

answers: Even Zion’s remains are precious to them
Zion has no value to them
They care only for its riches
challenge.explanation: Their affection extends even to the stones and dust of Zion.
challenge.q: What does the servants’ concern for Zion’s stones and dust show?

paragraphs.title: Salvation for Future Generations and Nations

easy.explanation: The psalm says, “This shall be written for the generation to come.”
easy.q: For whom shall these things be written?

easy.explanation: The LORD hears “the groaning of the prisoner.”
easy.q: Whose groaning does the LORD hear?

easy.explanation: The passage names both Zion and Jerusalem.
easy.q: Where will the name and praise of the LORD be declared?

answers: To hear the suffering and help those in distress
medium.explanation: He beholds the earth to hear the prisoner’s groaning and bring release.
medium.q: Why does the LORD look down from heaven?

medium.explanation: The people and kingdoms gather “to serve the LORD.”
medium.q: What will the gathered peoples and kingdoms do?

answers: A cry of pain or distress
medium.explanation: Groaning is a sound expressing suffering and distress.
medium.q: What does “groaning” mean in the phrase “the groaning of the prisoner”?

answers: So future people will praise the LORD for His works
So the deliverance will be forgotten
challenge.explanation: The coming generation and the people created will praise the LORD.
challenge.q: Why is the account written for future generations?

answers: God’s heavenly attention, help for the suffering, proclamation of His name, and the service of nations
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from God’s observation to deliverance and worldwide worship.
challenge.q: Which sequence best describes the movement of thought in these verses?

answers: God’s salvation reaches suffering individuals and whole peoples
Prisoners have no place in the passage
challenge.explanation: The verses mention both the release of prisoners and the gathering of kingdoms.
challenge.q: What does the connection between prisoners and kingdoms suggest?

paragraphs.title: A Plea to Live Until Redemption

answers: His strength is weakened and his days shortened
His strength is increased and his days lengthened
easy.explanation: He says, “He weakened my strength in the way; he shortened my days.”
easy.q: What has happened to the psalmist’s strength and days?

answers: Take him away in the midst of his days
easy.explanation: He asks, “take me not away in the midst of my days.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask God not to do?

easy.explanation: The psalmist says God’s years continue throughout all generations.

answers: The psalmist’s days are short, but God’s years continue through generations
The psalmist is eternal, but God is temporary
medium.explanation: The prayer is addressed to the eternal God by one whose days are shortened.
medium.q: What contrast is made between the psalmist and God?

answers: He hopes to live until God’s promised restoration
He wants to flee from God
He wants Zion to be forgotten
medium.explanation: His request expresses the desire to live long enough to see redemption.
medium.q: Why does the psalmist ask not to be taken away in the midst of his days?

answers: In the middle of my life
At the end of the world
At the beginning of the day
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to dying before one’s natural life is complete.
medium.q: What does “in the midst of my days” mean?

answers: The psalmist hopes to see God’s promised redemption
God will stop watching over His people
challenge.explanation: His plea suggests that he expects a future time of restoration.
challenge.q: What hope is implied in the request for more time?

answers: It turns from human weakness to a personal appeal to the enduring God
challenge.explanation: After describing weakness, the psalmist directly appeals to God for continued life.
challenge.q: How does the word “But” change the direction of the passage?

answers: He seeks lasting security from the One who does not perish
He thinks everything passes away equally
He does not believe God is eternal
challenge.explanation: The psalmist turns to God’s permanence while facing his own mortality.
challenge.q: What does addressing God as the one whose years span all generations reveal about the psalmist’s need?

paragraphs.title: God’s Eternity and the Endurance of His Servants’ Descendants

easy.explanation: The passage says, “Of old hast thou laid the foundation of the earth.”
easy.q: Who laid the foundation of the earth?

answers: They will grow old and be changed
They will disappear from the passage immediately
easy.explanation: They are compared to a garment that grows old and is changed.
easy.q: What will happen to the earth and heavens in the comparison to a garment?

answers: The children and seed of His servants
easy.explanation: The closing verse speaks of the children and seed of God’s servants.
easy.q: Who shall continue and be established before God?

answers: The world perishes and grows old, but the LORD endures
The LORD grows old, but the world endures
Both perish at the same time
medium.explanation: The passage says, “They shall perish, but thou shalt endure.”
medium.q: What is the main contrast between the LORD and the created world?

answers: God remains the same and His years have no end
medium.explanation: God’s unchanging and eternal nature provides the foundation for their continuance.
medium.q: Why is there hope for the children and descendants of God’s servants?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes the world becoming old like a worn garment.
medium.q: What does “wax old” mean in this passage?

answers: The created world changes and wears out, while God remains
People abandon the worship of God
challenge.explanation: The garment image represents the temporary and changeable nature of creation.
challenge.q: What does the image of changing a garment communicate?

answers: It moves from human weakness to God’s eternity and the hope of future generations
It cancels the poor person’s prayer
challenge.explanation: The psalm ends by contrasting fading humanity with God’s enduring care.
challenge.q: How does the ending reinforce the central message of the psalm?

answers: God’s unchanging nature provides a secure foundation for their future
God’s changing nature causes their destruction
challenge.explanation: Because God remains the same and has no end, His servants’ descendants can be established before Him.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between “thou art the same” and the continuance of God’s servants’ seed?
